prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which laid the foundation for incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: I have not changed my preferred configuration: a single prize part, B017, with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The round-1 exchange tested it from several directions and it held. The case is a continuous chain from gut-hormone physiology in humans, through proglucagon processing and the bioactive GLP-1(7-36) peptide, to a drug class with randomized outcome evidence in glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal endpoints. It is original, independently confirmed over decades and mature. The question the chair's summary put to us is whether the committee wants a physiology-centred citation. I do. The prize is for a discovery in physiology or medicine, and a citation anchored on the hormone's physiology and its active form is defensible on its own terms. The omission of Knudsen then becomes a stated principle: the award honours what was learned about the hormone, and the later analogue engineering is acknowledged by the wording 'laid the foundation for' therapies, not by a name.
statement.case_against: Credit remains the weak point and I do not think round 1 resolved it. The priority question for the active peptide between Mojsov and Habener and others cannot be settled from the supplied evidence, and naming Mojsov is a judgment under uncertainty, not a verified finding. Leaving out Knudsen means the people who made the drugs patients actually use are not named, and five of six members call that a real cost. A physiology-centred citation reduces that gap but does not remove it. There is also the standing risk that we are rewarding commercial scale as much as scientific originality, and the three-person limit prevents us from correcting any of this by adding names.

responses.point: Linnarsson moved from Knudsen to Mojsov but calls the choice a close call, and asks whether a physiology-centred citation can acknowledge the analogue drugs without making Knudsen necessary. She also argued that counting Knudsen's work as decisive would turn the Holst and Drucker part into a therapy story.
responses.response: I agree with the consistency argument. If analogue design is the decisive step, then the whole citation reads as a pharmaceutical award, and the committee would be crediting a different achievement than the one it says it is crediting. That is why I keep the wording 'laid the foundation for' therapies. It answers your question: the citation can point to the clinical consequence without making the engineering a credited contribution. I do not claim this closes the gap. Where I would push back is on calling the Mojsov versus Knudsen choice close. The priority dispute argues for naming the person who is central to the active peptide, and I find that more defensible than naming a development step that builds on it.

responses.point: Sandberg keeps B024 only as an alternative, not as a second part, because a split prize would force the B017 union below the three names she thinks it needs, and she ranks B024 a little lower than I do because the Philadelphia chromosome and BCR-ABL discoveries lie outside the credited names.
responses.response: Your arithmetic is right and I now accept it. The three-person limit applies to the whole configuration, so a second part with Druker, Lydon and Sawyers would cost B017 its trio, and I would not trade Holst, Drucker or Mojsov away for it. My own round-1 position was that B024 is cleaner than I implied, but your point about the uncredited upstream work is the same concern I raised about consistency with Perlmann: if we hold GLP-1 to a physiology standard, imatinib has to meet it too, and it meets it less well. I therefore drop the idea of B024 as a paired part and keep it as an alternative for a later year.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius moved off Knudsen after reading colleagues and would handle Knudsen's contribution in the citation wording, and she still lists B018 (anti-TNF) as an alternative, arguing that Feldmann and Maini showed in human synovium that TNF drives the cytokine cascade and then proved that blocking it works.
responses.response: Your description of the synovial work is fairer than my round-1 summary, and I accept that it is more than translation. It does not change my configuration, though. The competing claims you name (Kollias, Cerami, Vilcek and the antibody engineers) mean any two-person B018 is attribution-incomplete, and within the three-person total there is no room to add them. I therefore do not support it as a second part this year. On the wording, I take your suggestion that the citation carry the analogue step so the omission is principled, and my revised citation moves in that direction.

responses.point: El Manira cites central appetite effects as part of the B017 case and frames the choice as whether the committee rewards discovery or development, noting that Linnarsson's Knudsen configuration better captures why the therapies exist.
responses.response: We agree on the central framing, discovery rather than development. On the appetite effects I keep my position: the case should rest on the peripheral incretin physiology and the outcome data, because the CNS mechanism of weight loss is still being worked out, and a citation that asserted it would claim more than the evidence supports. For that reason my citation does not mention appetite or the brain. I would not object if the committee wrote the weight indication into the citation through the word 'obesity', as the current wording does.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active peptide can be defended against Habener and others. I cannot resolve it from the supplied evidence and I treat her inclusion as a judgment under uncertainty.
Whether the committee accepts a physiology-centred citation with Knudsen omitted as a principle, or sees it as an oversight that weakens the award.

Whether any second part could ever be added within the three-person limit without breaking the B017 trio. At present I see none with a complete attribution, with the Eshhar gap for B006 and the uncredited upstream work for B024 as the main obstacles.
statement.conflict_note: No change. No specific conflict is apparent for any shortlisted ballot from my profile. For transparency, my profile records about twenty co-authored works with Thomas Perlmann (dopamine neurons, Nurr1, autophagy), a collegial connection outside the candidates under discussion, and a postdoctoral period with Paul Greengard that does not bear on any shortlisted candidate. I note that other members have disclosed ties to each other, none involving a shortlisted candidate, and no member has requested recusal.
